description: Same as the paper-traded baseline (12-1 lookback, 20 equal-weighted stocks, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average), with one change: stocks are ranked on 12-1 return divided by annualised volatility instead of raw return.
hypothesis: Raw momentum rankings favour high-volatility stocks whose past return is partly noise and which drive momentum crashes (Barroso & Santa-Clara; Daniel & Moskowitz). Ranking on return per unit of volatility picks steadier trends, the same normalisation NSE uses for Nifty200 Momentum 30. It should cut drawdowns and turnover and raise return per rupee at risk. Only one knob changes, so any lead over the baseline is less likely to be fitted noise.
lessons: On NIFTY 200, raw 12-1 strength is the main source of the edge. Penalising volatility at the ranking stage removes the high-momentum winners that drive the big years. A 3-point smaller drawdown does not pay for a 2.4% a year return drag. If volatility is used at all, it should control risk, through position size, and not decide which stocks get picked.
title: Volatility-adjusted 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-2.37% a year against it)

change_note: Ranking goes back to raw 12-1 return, the same as the baseline, and volatility now sets sizing only (inverse_volatility). This keeps the stock selection and aims to cut drawdown. The 60-day window and 2x cap cannot be set in this format, so the engine defaults apply.
description: Same selection as the baseline: the top 20 NIFTY 200 stocks by 12-1 return, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. Only the sizing changes, to inverse volatility. The format has no keys for the 60-day window or the 2x cap, so those come from the engine's inverse_volatility defaults and may differ from the request.
hypothesis: Version 1 lost return because ranking by return over volatility swapped strong winners for calmer, weaker names. Keeping the raw 12-1 ranking keeps those winners. Sizing by inverse volatility should give less weight to the stocks most prone to crashes (the momentum crash effect) and trim drawdowns without changing which stocks are held. Expect a worst fall below 23% with a return close to the baseline. A t of 2 or more over the baseline is unlikely, because the holdings are identical and only the weights differ.
lessons: Within a 20-stock momentum basket, volatility is part of the return source, so down-weighting it gives up return for only a slight cut in drawdown. Weighting tweaks inside the same selection move results by a couple of percent and tend to cost more than they save. A bigger difference is more likely to come from what is selected or from when the strategy goes to cash than from how positions are sized. The baseline remains the version to beat.
title: Raw 12-1 momentum, top 20, inverse-volatility sizing, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-2.28% a year against it)

change_note: Back to the baseline's raw 12-1 score and equal weights, since volatility-scaling lost return twice. Concentrated from 20 to 12 stocks to capture the stronger top-rank premium, with an own-200-day trend check per stock to keep crash-prone names out.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 on 12-1 momentum and hold the top 12 equally weighted, but only stocks still closing above their own 200-session average. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. Monthly rebalance. The only changes from the baseline are concentration and a per-stock trend check.
hypothesis: Both volatility-scaling attempts cut drawdown but also cut return, so risk-dampening is the wrong direction for beating the baseline. The momentum premium is strongest in the top ranks: the spread between the top and next deciles is well documented, so holding 12 instead of 20 should raise return. Concentration adds stock-specific crash risk. Requiring each stock to be above its own 200-session average drops names whose long-run winner status is already rolling over, which is the main source of momentum crashes. That should keep the worst fall under 30%.
lessons: Fewer stocks is mostly a variance dial on the same signal. It adds return in a few trend years and does not improve consistency or drawdown. Testing more position counts (10, 15) would be searching for a lucky parameter and undermines the pre-registered test. The paper-traded 20-stock baseline stays the rule, and later ideas should add independent information rather than retune holdings count.
title: Concentrated 12-1 momentum, 12 stocks, own-trend confirmation

training.why_not: its lead over the paper-traded rule could be luck: t = 1.65 (needs 2)

change_note: Added a 50-session own-trend filter to the baseline. It is a selection change that brings recent-trend information the 12-1 score ignores. Holdings count, weighting and ranking are left alone, per earlier lessons.
description: Paper-traded baseline (12-1 raw momentum, top 20, equal weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average). One change: a stock is eligible only if it closes above its own 50-session average. The ranking, holdings count, sizing and market filter are unchanged.
hypothesis: 12-1 momentum skips the latest month, so it keeps buying stocks whose trend has already broken. Those are where momentum crashes start. A 200-day own-trend filter adds little, because a top-decile 12-month winner is almost always above its 200-day average. A 50-day filter adds independent, recent information: it drops names already rolling over and passes the slot to the next-ranked stock in an intact trend. If this works, the lead should come from fewer losses in choppy years (2011, 2013, 2018, 2019, 2022), not from a few trend years. Risk: it may clash with short-term reversal and add turnover, so a t below 2 is a likely result.
lessons: A per-stock short-trend filter on top of 12-1 momentum is mostly redundant, because top-momentum stocks are already above their trends. Its main effect is extra turnover and early exits in trending markets. Making the filter slower would mostly bring the result back to the baseline rather than beat it. Any real improvement probably has to come from a different dimension, such as ranking quality, volatility-adjusted momentum, or position sizing, not from more exit filters.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, 50-day own-trend confirmation, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-0.57% a year against it)

change_note: Dropped the 50-day own-trend filter, which added nothing (-0.57%/yr). Added a loose 50% volatility cap to exclude only crash-prone extreme names, while keeping raw-return ranking, which earlier tests showed is the edge.
description: Same paper-traded rule: rank NIFTY 200 on 12-1 return, hold top 20 equal-weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. One change: stocks with annualised volatility above 50% are not eligible. Ranking stays raw return, so this only removes the extreme tail, not ordinary high-volatility winners.
hypothesis: Momentum crashes (Daniel-Moskowitz) concentrate in the highest-volatility, lottery-like losers-turned-winners, often junk rebounds after selloffs. Earlier tests showed that penalising volatility across the whole ranking cuts the winners that drive returns. A loose cap instead removes only the extreme tail, which tends to give back gains in reversals. Expect similar trend-year returns with fewer sharp single-name losses. This is one knob set from theory, not a sweep. A t>=2 lead is unlikely, so read a fail as evidence that the baseline is robust.
lessons: In this universe, momentum's edge comes from the high-volatility, crash-prone names, so filtering on crash risk cuts the right tail without trimming the left tail. Drawdown is already set by the market-level 200-day filter, so stock-level risk screens don't move worst fall. Future ideas should either add return (better ranking or timing) or attack drawdown at the portfolio or regime level, not exclude stocks.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, exclude crash-prone names (vol cap 50%), NIFTY 200d

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-5.32% a year against it)

change_note: Lookback cut from 12 to 6 months, nothing else changed: tests whether a faster formation window, as used in NSE's own momentum index, catches leadership changes earlier.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 stocks on their 6-month return, skipping the latest month. Hold the top 20 equally weighted and rebalance monthly. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-session average. Only the lookback differs from the paper-traded baseline.
hypothesis: NSE's own momentum index blends 6- and 12-month returns, and emerging-market momentum tends to be shorter-lived than US momentum. A 6-1 window should pick up new leadership after regime shifts such as 2009, 2014, 2020 and 2023 sooner. It should also drop fading 12-month winners earlier. Earlier tests showed volatility screens and weighting only remove return, so this changes what is selected, not how it is filtered or sized. Expect higher yearly return than 12-1 at similar drawdown under the same market filter. Risk: more turnover at 0.2%.
lessons: A shorter lookback adds turnover and cost without adding edge. Its wins cluster in sharp-recovery years, which looks like timing luck. The 12-1 signal with the 200-day filter is hard to beat by retuning the lookback. Cutting costs and turnover, or adding an independent signal, is more promising than changing the horizon.
title: 6-1 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (shorter formation)

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-1.25% a year against it)

change_note: Market filter shortened from 200 to 100 sessions; selection and sizing left as in the paper rule. Earlier lessons say gains are more likely to come from when the strategy goes to cash than from re-weighting or re-ranking.
description: Same selection as the paper rule: 12-1 return, top 20, equal weight. The only change is the market filter. It holds cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 100-session average instead of its 200-session average. This tests the timing of going to cash, the one lever earlier days flagged but never tried.
hypothesis: Momentum losses cluster in sharp market reversals: fast sell-offs (2011, 2018, Feb-Mar 2020) and V-shaped rebounds (2009, mid-2020). The 200-day average reacts late on both sides, so the basket takes much of the fall and then sits in cash through the early recovery. A 100-day trend is still a standard trend signal but turns about twice as fast. It should exit earlier and re-enter sooner, lifting return over the baseline without adding a selection knob. The cost is more switches at 0.2% each and more false exits in choppy years. Prior odds of reaching t >= 2 on one timing change are modest.
lessons: Making the market-trend filter faster just trades V-recovery gains for whipsaw losses in trending years, so the net is about zero. The baseline's 200-day filter is not the bottleneck. Small drawdown improvements of 1-2 points are within noise and do not justify replacing a rule already being paper-traded. With one version left, tweaking filter speed again is unlikely to produce a significant lead.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, faster NIFTY 100-day cash filter
